title: AI is hitting entry-level jobs hardest, Stanford study finds
gist: Stanford's updated 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' paper finds employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations is now 19 percent below their less-exposed peers, up from a 13 percent gap a year earlier, while economy-wide employment shows little difference. The mechanism is reduced hiring rather than firings, concentrated in occupations where AI use is automative rather than augmentative and where the work rests on codified rather than tacit knowledge — a labor market that holds its headline level while closing the career on-ramp.

themes.theme: The entry-level gap and its trajectory

insights.claim: Employment levels for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations are now 19 percent below those of peers in less-exposed fields, up from a 13 percent gap measured a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A six-point widening in one year is the single hardest number showing AI labor displacement is accelerating, not stabilizing.
insights.quote: employment levels for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most “AI-exposed” occupations are now 19 percent below those of their peers in fields less exposed to AI disruption

insights.claim: Since 2022, employment for workers aged 22 to 25 fell about 11 percent in the top 40 percent of AI-impacted jobs while growing 10 percent in the 60 percent of jobs with the least AI impact.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The absolute decline in exposed roles, alongside growth in unexposed ones, means this is reallocation of young labor rather than a general hiring recession.

insights.claim: Crunching the numbers economy-wide, researchers found little to no difference in relative overall employment between the jobs judged most and least affected by AI — the effect only appears once entry-level workers are separated out.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Aggregate employment statistics are structurally blind to this effect — headline payroll numbers will not signal it until the cohort ages through.

insights.claim: Older workers appear largely unaffected so far, making the disruption a cohort effect rather than an occupation-wide one.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Incumbency is protective — which means the political constituency for AI labor policy is young and currently unorganized.

insights.claim: The phenomenon manifests mainly through lower hiring rates for entry-level workers in AI-impacted fields rather than through increased firings or employees quitting.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Displacement shows up in the hiring funnel, so job-openings and new-grad placement data lead layoff data as an AI-impact indicator.

insights.claim: Labor market effects among 22-to-25-year-olds appear as lower overall employment rather than reduced pay rates, meaning wages are not adjusting to clear the market.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Quantity adjustment without price adjustment implies the roles are being eliminated, not repriced — cheaper juniors would not restore the jobs.

insights.claim: Researchers used a large subsample of anonymized high-frequency payroll data from HR management company ADP, rating occupational AI exposure with both a prior labor-market-impact gauge and Anthropic's Economic Index of actual Claude usage by occupation.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Actual model-usage telemetry, not survey-based exposure guesses, is now the measurement standard for AI labor research.

themes.theme: Automative versus augmentative use as the dividing line

insights.claim: Anthropic's Economic Index distinguishes automative queries that fully replace human work from augmentative ones that help workers be more effective, and jobs where automation-oriented use is prevalent show the worst relative entry-level employment.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The automative/augmentative split is the usable screen for which occupations face displacement versus productivity uplift.
insights.quote: The findings are consistent with automation-oriented uses of AI substituting for labor while complementary uses are associated with flat or rising employment

insights.claim: Accountants and auditors and receptionists and information clerks ranked among the occupations most susceptible to AI automation, while chief executives and registered nurses were among those using AI most augmentatively.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Named occupations give a concrete map of where entry-level hiring pipelines are closing versus holding.

insights.claim: For jobs where AI is merely augmentative, the entry-level employment picture is much more muddled, with flat or rising employment rather than clear decline.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Augmentation is not currently destroying entry-level jobs, which supports selective rather than blanket pessimism about AI-exposed sectors.

insights.claim: The researchers theorize entry-level workers are especially vulnerable in jobs built on codified knowledge — formal, standardized, documented knowledge teachable through education, textbooks, or written procedures — while AI complements experienced workers' tacit knowledge acquired through practice, mentorship, and repeated exposure.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The most durable heuristic in the paper: work that can be written down is exactly the work AI substitutes for, which is precisely what juniors are hired to do.

insights.claim: Using O*NET's required formal education level as a proxy for codified knowledge, the data show occupations with higher codified knowledge have slower entry-level employment growth while occupations with higher tacit knowledge have faster employment growth for mid-career and senior workers.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The same variable that hurts juniors helps seniors — AI is widening the experience premium within occupations, not just across them.

insights.claim: Higher education still buffers the effect: occupations with a higher share of college graduates showed more muted differences between more- and less-exposed jobs, whereas in jobs with few college graduates the least-exposed occupations grew and the most-exposed declined.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland

themes.theme: Forward view from the lead researcher

insights.claim: Erik Brynjolfsson warns of a near future where jobs for those employed in the pre-AI era largely persist while many jobs for the incoming working-age cohort disappear, describing the entry-level effects as real, persistent, and widening.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A stable-headline, closed-on-ramp labor market is a scenario that breaks conventional recession signals and delays political response.
insights.quote: I’m more worried than I was about a labor market that keeps its overall employment level while quietly closing the on-ramp for people starting their careers.

insights.claim: The August 2026 edition of the paper updates and revises last year's version with fresh data and refined statistics, and finds the previously identified entry-level trends persisting and expanding rather than reversing.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Replication with a second year of data raises confidence that this is a structural trend and not a 2022–2023 hiring-cycle artifact.
